contributions.headingText: Infantile fibrosarcoma (IFS) is a malignant fibroblastic tumour most commonly occurring in infancy, frequently characterized by an ETV6-NTRK3 fusion. It is a locally aggressive and rapidly growing tumour that only rarely metastasizes.
2B5F.2 & XH7BC6 Sarcoma, not elsewhere classified of other specified sites & Infantile fibrosarcoma
Acceptable: congenital fibrosarcoma; infantile fibrosarcoma-like tumour; cellular congenital mesoblastic nephroma.

The most common sites of involvement are the superficial and deep soft tissues of the extremities, followed by the trunk and the head and neck. Less commonly, IFS arises in the abdomen or retroperitoneum {19917847; 974993; 8159611} and rarely in skeletal or visceral locations (e.g. lung, bowel) {21843073; 25150723}. Analogous tumours in the kidney are designated cellular congenital mesoblastic nephroma {9823307}.

IFS typically manifests as a localized, rapidly enlarging, painless mass or swelling, or as an exophytic nodule {974993}. One third of cases are found at birth {974993} and 14% are detected at prenatal ultrasound {19917847}. IFS may ulcerate the skin surface and resemble vascular tumours {16918626}. Intratumoural haemorrhage in utero or in neonates may lead to anaemia or haemorrhagic shock {21618315; 19018145}. Imaging shows a heterogeneously enhancing mass with nonspecific characteristics that sometimes contains haemorrhage {24706181}.

More than 75% of cases occur in the first year of life, 15% in the second year, and < 10% in older children {974993; 19917847}. Some of the tumours with alternative kinase fusions have been reported in older children {28877062; 30585824}. IFS has a slight male predominance {974993; 19917847}.

IFS is driven by oncogenic activation of kinase signalling, mostly as a result of in-frame fusions upstream of the kinase domains and in rare cases due to complex activating mutations {29915264}. Most cases harbour the canonical ETV6-NTRK3 fusion resulting from t(12;15)(p13;q25), although rare cases involving other partners, such as EML4-NTRK3, have been reported {29099503; 30585824}. In addition, alternative fusions involving other kinases have been reported in a subset of cases, including NTRK1, NTRK2, BRAF, and MET {30585824; 28877062; 29915264; 28510278}. NTRK1 fusion gene partners include TPM3, LMNA, TPR, SQSTM1, and MIR584F1 {28877062; 30585824}. BRAF fusions and complex deletions have been described, which probably result in the loss of the negative regulatory RAS-binding domain, resulting in constitutive activation of BRAF {28877062; 29915264}. A single case with TFG-MET fusion has been reported {28510278}. The genetic abnormalities of cellular congenital mesoblastic nephroma share substantial overlap, in keeping with a common pathogenesis {9823307; 29099503; 29915264}. Secretory carcinomas of the breast and salivary gland also harbour the ETV6-NTRK3 fusion {12450792; 26291510; 28060365}.

Tumours vary in size but can be quite large (median size: 5–6 cm; range: 1 to > 15 cm) {561651; 30585824}. Grossly, they are typically poorly circumscribed, with infiltrative borders into surrounding structures; some tumours may have a thin pseudocapsule.

Histologically, IFS can display a broad morphological spectrum. Most commonly, it is a cellular neoplasm composed of monomorphic spindled to ovoid cells with scant cytoplasm and slightly angulated nuclei. The cells may be arranged in randomly oriented compact sheets or in herringbone fascicles. The background stroma can range from collagenous to myxoid. A prominent haemangiopericytoma-like vascular pattern is often present. Tumours with decreased cellularity and prominent collagen resembling fibromatosis or myofibromatosis can also be seen {22420727; 30585824}. A rich mixed chronic inflammatory infiltrate may be present. Infiltrative growth into and entrapping adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, and other structures is common. Mitoses range from infrequent to numerous, without prognostic significance; no atypical mitoses are seen. Patchy necrosis may be present. The immunohistochemical profile is nonspecific, with variable expression of SMA, CD34, S100, and desmin {22420727; 30585824}. IFSs with NTRK gene rearrangements are often positive by immunohistochemistry using a pan-TRK antibody {29863809; 29683818}.
ETV6-NTRK3 or other gene fusions/rearrangements can be demonstrated by a variety of molecular approaches {10895816; 11684968; 30585824}.

Essential: the majority of patients are aged < 2 years; spindle to primitive ovoid/round cell tumour; often arranged in a fascicular/herringbone pattern; staghorn vasculature and mixed inflammation.

Desirable: ETV6-NTRK3 fusion or other rearrangements involving NTRK1, BRAF, and MET.

IFS is locally aggressive but with relatively infrequent metastases and an overall favourable outcome. The overall 10-year survival rate for IFS with standard treatment regimens (various combinations of surgery and/or standard chemotherapy) is about 90% {974993; 561651; 19917847}. Reported local recurrence rates are 25–40%, with recurrence highly associated with incomplete resection {19917847; 30585824}. However, for many tumours, complete surgical resection would result in substantial morbidity and is therefore not the ideal management. The rate of metastasis is 8–15% {30585824; 19917847; 561651}. Rare cases of spontaneous tumour regression have been observed {29200168}. The advent of targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors may alter the prognosis and clinical management of this disease in advanced or intractable disease {29606586; 30204247}.
